origin_region: Saga · Ureshino; Nagasaki · Sonogi; Kumamoto; some Shizuoka
cultivar: Yabukita, Saemidori, Okumidori; Yutaka Midori in Kyushu lots
processing: Steamed like sencha but the final straightening roll is skipped, so the leaf is dried in a rotating drum and ends up curled into a comma shape; a pan-fired version (kama-guri) is made the same way with a hot pan in place of the steamer.
harvest_season: First flush (late April–May) for the good grades, with the first lots sold as shincha; second flush goes into everyday bags.
appearance_dry: Short, curled, comma-shaped leaves in dark green, chunkier than sencha needles.
appearance_wet: Curled leaves that open into small whole pieces.
taste_profile: Round, smooth and sweet with less astringency than sencha, a gentle umami and a clean, slightly fruity aroma.

brewing.notes: Brew like sencha; the curled leaf is a little slower to open, so give the first steep a full minute. Forgiving with hotter water, which brings out a nuttier side.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's harvest by Kyushu producers, mostly first flush (ichibancha), with the first lots appearing as shincha in late April; Ureshino-cha and Sonogi-cha are the regional labels to look for. It is treated exactly like sencha for storage: sealed, cold, finished within the year.
description:
Tamaryokucha, usually called guricha, is the curly green tea of Kyushu: Ureshino in Saga, Sonogi in Nagasaki and parts of Kumamoto make most of it, with a little from Shizuoka. Instead of a sencha's straight needle the leaf is a short comma, and the cup is rounder and softer, which is why people who find sencha sharp often end up here.

The difference is one missing step. Steamed tamaryokucha (mushi-guri) is steamed and rolled like sencha but skips the final straightening roll; the leaf is finished in a rotating drum instead, where it curls up as it dries. The pan-fired version (kama-guri) does the same thing with a hot pan in place of the steamer and is really a kamairicha. Less pressure on the leaf means less cell damage and a milder, less astringent cup with a gentle umami and a clean, lightly fruity aroma. The steamed style was developed in the early twentieth century, originally with export markets in mind, and became the signature of the Ureshino and Sonogi districts.

Brew it as you would sencha, 5 g for 150 ml at 70–75 °C; give the first steep a full minute because the curled leaf takes a moment to open, then a short second and a longer third. It is forgiving of hotter water, which brings out a more roasted, nutty side, and it cold-brews well. It rarely turns bitter, so it is a safe tea to serve to guests who do not know Japanese tea.

Look for Ureshino-cha or Sonogi-cha on the label, which almost always means guricha, and for first flush; the first lots are sold as shincha from late April. Yabukita, Saemidori and Okumidori are the usual cultivars. Prices are modest for the quality, because the district has less name recognition than Uji or Shizuoka, and that is an opportunity. It is stored and drunk like sencha, within the year.

Try it against a sencha from the same cultivar to see what the final rolling step does to the taste.
sources_note: The export-origin story of steamed guricha (early 20th century, Russian/Soviet market) is widely repeated in the trade; stated vaguely here.
